t: LeetCode 2432 — The Employee That Worked on the Longest Task
o: Each task starts exactly when the previous one ends, and task 0 starts at time 0. So the duration of task i is simply `leaveTime[i] - leaveTime[i-1]` (with `prev = 0` for the first task). We need the employee whose single task has the maximum duration, breaking ties by smallest id. In Example 1, durations are 3, 2, 4, 6 → employee 1 wins. In Example 3, durations are 10 and 10; both employees tie, so we return id 0. Constraints are tiny (≤500 entries), so a single linear scan suffices.
k: Task duration is just the difference between consecutive leave times: `logs[i][1] - logs[i-1][1]`, with previous time initialized to 0.
A single pass tracking (best duration, best id) with strict `>` comparison automatically resolves ties toward the smaller id since we scan left to right.
The parameter n is not actually needed for the computation.

a.n: Approach 1: Single Pass with Running Maximum
a.i: Iterate through the logs once, computing each task's duration as the gap from the previous leave time. Keep the best duration seen so far and its employee id. Using a strictly greater comparison means an equal later duration never replaces an earlier one, guaranteeing the smallest id among ties is returned.
s: For each log [id, t], compute dur = t - prev, then set prev = t.
If dur > bestDur, update bestDur = dur and ans = id.
a.t: O(m) where m = logs.length — one pass over the logs with constant work per entry.
a.sp: O(1) — only a few scalar variables are used.

a.n: Approach 2: Precompute All Durations Then Scan
a.i: First build an array of durations by diffing consecutive leave times, then find the index of the maximum duration using any max-scan (or Python's max with key). This separates 'derive durations' from 'pick winner', which some find clearer. Tie-breaking still favors the earliest index when scanning left to right or using max's first-occurrence behavior.
s: Create array durs of length m; set durs[0] = logs[0][1] and durs[i] = logs[i][1] - logs[i-1][1].
Find the index of the first occurrence of the maximum value in durs.
Return logs at that index's employee id.
a.t: O(m) — two passes over the data (build durations, find max).
a.sp: O(m) — extra array to store all durations.

w: In an interview, go straight to Approach 1: it is optimal in time and space and trivially correct. The main pitfall is forgetting that the first task starts at time 0, so its duration equals its own leave time — initialize prev to 0. Another subtle point is tie-breaking: use strict `>` when updating the best so earlier ids win ties naturally; reversing to `>=` would break Example 3. Edge cases include a single log entry and all durations being equal. Likely follow-ups: what if logs were unsorted (sort by leave time first), or if you needed the top-k hardest workers (use a heap after computing durations).
